story.headline: The dollar held onto its gains from hot US inflation figures through Asian trading, with a December Federal Reserve hike now close to fully priced. Oil edged up as tanker attacks near Hormuz went on.

reads.policy: Markets now treat a December Federal Reserve hike as close to certain, and a second hike early next year as more likely than not. Fed officials keep leaning that way, which widens the gap between US rates and most others. Japan and the euro area are expected to hike in December too, but that is already priced.
reads.growth: Australian home lending slumped in the third quarter, a sign high rates there are biting hard. The US economy still looks firmer than Australia's, Canada's or New Zealand's, a split that favours the dollar. UK growth figures on Thursday are the next big read.
reads.inflation: US inflation is running at roughly twice the Fed's goal, and no new figures landed overnight to change that. That keeps the Fed hiking, which supports the dollar and weighs on gold. US producer prices on Friday are the next check.
reads.risk: Asian markets stayed calm overnight, so there was little demand for safe havens. The franc and the yen stayed weak against the dollar as a result. Tanker attacks in the Gulf are the main thing that could change the mood quickly.
reads.tot: Oil bounced off its lowest level in two months as attacks on ships near the Strait of Hormuz continued. Prices are still far below October's peak, which eases the energy bill for Japan and the euro area. Firmer oil gives the Canadian dollar a little support.
reads.positioning: Hedge funds lean toward the dollar and the yen and against the kiwi, the Canadian dollar and the euro, with big recent additions to bets against the kiwi and the euro. The dollar's rise this week has gone with those bets, so there is no sign of a squeeze. The next weekly report is due Friday.
reads.fiscal: Weak demand at two US government bond sales this week pushed long-term US borrowing costs up, which supports the dollar for now. The worry is that buyers want more pay to hold US debt. A 30-year bond sale on Thursday is the next check.

fed.summary: The Federal Reserve held rates on October 28 with two officials voting to hike. Hot October inflation figures have made a December hike close to certain, and some officials want more after that, which supports the dollar.
fed.priced: December: hike close to certain, a half-point move a small chance; January: another hike more likely than not.
fed.why: US inflation is running at about twice the Fed's 2% goal and hiring was strong in October. Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan says at least two more hikes are needed, and Governor Christopher Waller has raised a half-point move.
fed.watch: US producer prices on Friday at 7:30 AM CT and what Fed officials say about the size and number of hikes. The decision is December 9.

boc.summary: The Bank of Canada raised rates to 2.50% in October and has said more hikes may be needed. Notes from that meeting showed a real debate but no new signal, and bets on a December hike sit at about one in three.
boc.priced: December: hold is the base case; hike about one in three.
boc.why: Dearer energy lifted Canadian inflation and the bank expects it to stay near 3% for over a year, but the job market keeps weakening. That gives it reasons to move slowly.
boc.watch: Oil prices and how far US rates pull ahead of Canada's, before the December 9 decision.

rbnz.summary: The Reserve Bank of New Zealand held at 2.75% in October in a 4–3 vote, though members agreed more tightening is likely. Rising unemployment has cut bets on a December hike to below even.
rbnz.priced: December: hike less likely than not.
rbnz.why: Price pressures argue for a hike, but unemployment at its highest since 2015 argues for patience.
rbnz.watch: Whether stocks stay calm, the official election result on November 27, and what the next government means for the budget, before the December 9 decision.

ecb.summary: The European Central Bank held its deposit rate at 2.50% in October, and markets expect a hike in December. Because that hike is already expected, it gives the euro little fresh support.
ecb.why: Euro-area inflation is about double the goal, mostly because of energy, but shoppers are cutting back and borrowing costs have already risen. That makes the bank wary of doing too much.
ecb.watch: President Christine Lagarde speaks Wednesday at 3:45 AM CT and Thursday at 1:30 PM CT, and euro-area growth figures follow Friday at 4:00 AM CT, before the December 17 decision.

boj.summary: The Bank of Japan held at 1.25% in October, and its meeting notes show several members want to raise rates faster. Markets expect a December hike, but rising US yields keep widening the gap that weakens the yen.
boj.why: Inflation has been running above the 2% goal, and some members see the rate that neither speeds up nor slows the economy well above today's level. Weak household spending is the main reason others want to go slowly.
boj.watch: Japanese wholesale prices on Wednesday at 5:50 PM CT and how far US yields climb. The decision is December 18.

rba.summary: The Reserve Bank of Australia raised rates to 4.85% on November 3, the highest since 2008, but three members wanted to wait. Weak consumer confidence and a slump in home lending since then support the case for a pause.
rba.priced: December: no firm pricing yet; the bank itself hinted at a pause.
rba.why: Inflation is still too high, but households are feeling the rate rises, with new home loans falling sharply, and the board is split. So the bank wants to see how its hikes work first.
rba.watch: Australian jobs figures for October next week, and the mood in global stock markets, before the December 8 decision.

boe.summary: The Bank of England raised Bank Rate to 4.00% on November 5, its first hike since 2023. Governor Andrew Bailey said it is unlikely to be the last unless the Middle East conflict ends, and his deputy Clare Lombardelli has not ruled out December.
boe.priced: December: a second hike possible; no firm pricing yet.
boe.why: Energy and fuel costs have pushed UK inflation to its highest in about a year, and several officials want more hikes.
boe.watch: UK growth figures on Thursday at 1:00 AM CT, and oil prices, before the December 17 decision. Cheaper oil would weaken the case for a second hike.

snb.summary: The Swiss National Bank holds its rate at zero and says it can still sell francs if they get too strong. Higher October inflation has made another cut less likely, and markets mostly expect a hold in December.
snb.why: Inflation is low and a strong franc keeps import prices down, so the bank has no reason to hike. October's rise in inflation makes a cut less pressing.
snb.watch: How far the franc moves as war fears ease, and the mood in stock markets, before the December 10 decision.

USD.summary: The dollar sits in the middle of the board: rate and inflation support are partly offset by a Democratic Congress. Hot October inflation figures have made a December Fed hike close to certain, which keeps it firm.

notes.policy: A December Fed hike looks close to certain after hot inflation figures, and some officials want more hikes after that.
notes.inflation: US core inflation has run at about twice the Fed's goal for three months, which keeps pressure on it to raise rates.
notes.fiscal: With Democrats controlling Congress, President Trump's spending plans look harder to pass, which trims some support for the dollar.

EUR.summary: The euro sits near the bottom of the board: weak growth, dear energy and France's debt worries outweigh an expected December rate hike. It fell back as hot US inflation figures lifted the dollar.

notes.policy: A December European Central Bank hike is expected, but euro rates still sit below US and UK rates, so the gap works against the euro.
notes.growth: Business surveys and shoppers in the euro area have weakened, with France's economy shrinking again.
notes.inflation: Euro-area inflation is about double the bank's goal, which keeps a December hike on the table.
notes.tot: The euro area buys most of its energy abroad, so dear oil drains money out of the region, though the recent fall in prices eases that.
notes.positioning: Speculators hold one of their biggest bets against the euro in years, so good news could set off a sharp rebound as they close it.
notes.fiscal: France's high debt and shaky budget keep investors demanding extra pay to hold French bonds, which weighs on the euro.

GBP.summary: The pound sits near the top of the board after the Bank of England raised rates to 4.00% and signalled more may follow. A firmer Fed has trimmed that edge, and UK growth figures on Thursday will test it.

notes.policy: The Bank of England hiked in November, and its governor said it is unlikely to be the last while the Middle East conflict lasts.
notes.growth: UK business surveys have been the strongest since February, even though shoppers have pulled back.
notes.inflation: UK inflation is at its highest in about a year, keeping pressure on the Bank of England.

JPY.summary: The yen sits low on the board because Japanese rates are far below others and Japan pays dearly for imported energy. A likely December rate hike gives it some support, but a firmer Fed keeps the dollar near 159 yen.

notes.policy: At 1.25%, the Bank of Japan's rate is far below other major banks, even though a December hike is likely and some members want faster rises.
notes.risk: The yen tends to gain when stock markets get scared, as they did last week, and loses some of that pull when they calm.
notes.tot: Japan buys almost all its energy abroad, so dear oil weighs on the yen, though the recent fall in prices eases that.
notes.positioning: Speculators hold one of their biggest bets on the yen in years, which could unwind fast if the mood turns.

CHF.summary: The franc sits in the middle of the board: its safe-haven pull is offset by inflation too low to need higher rates. The Swiss National Bank also says it can sell francs if they get too strong.

notes.inflation: Swiss inflation is low, so the central bank has no need to raise rates from zero.
notes.risk: The franc draws money when markets get nervous, but with fear low it has had little of that support lately.

AUD.summary: The Aussie scores well on the board thanks to the highest rates among the major central banks and firm commodity prices. It still trades mostly on stock-market mood and US rates, and slowing at home argues for a pause.

notes.policy: Australia's interest rate is the highest among the major central banks, though the governor hinted at a pause.
notes.growth: Australian unemployment is at a five-year high and home lending has slumped, though China's stronger buying helps exporters.
notes.inflation: Inflation is running above the Reserve Bank of Australia's forecasts, which kept it hiking.
notes.tot: Australia sells commodities abroad, and firm prices support its earnings.
notes.positioning: Speculators are betting heavily against the Aussie, so better news could set off a sharp rebound as they close those bets.

CAD.summary: The Canadian dollar sits mid-board: the Bank of Canada's October hike and oil exports help, but job losses have cut bets on more hikes. A firmer Fed has kept it near its weakest against the US dollar since mid-October.

notes.policy: The Bank of Canada raised rates in October and says more may be needed, though its meeting notes added no new signal and markets doubt a December move.
notes.growth: Canada lost jobs in September and October, and growth has stalled.
notes.inflation: Rising costs for Canadian producers point to more inflation ahead.
notes.tot: Canada exports oil, so prices still well above last year support its earnings, though the slide from October's highs trims that help.

NZD.summary: The kiwi sits low on the board because rising unemployment has cut bets on a December rate hike. It bounced after an election count pointed to the same government staying, but slipped again as US yields rose.

notes.growth: New Zealand's unemployment rose to its highest since 2015.
notes.tot: Firm prices for dairy, New Zealand's main export, and stronger Chinese buying support its earnings.
notes.positioning: Speculators are betting heavily against the kiwi, so better news could set off a sharp rebound as they close those bets.
